articles.title: Carbon dioxide is a climate problem. It might also be a laundry solution.
articles.content:
Doing the laundry has grown easier and more efficient over the years, yet two things have always remained the same: A washing machine needs water, and a dryer needs heat. Technology designed to clean aerospace parts reimagines the process by ditching both of those in favor of an unlikely substitute: carbon dioxide, the very gas we’re trying so hard to contain.

Under pressure, CO2 becomes a low-viscosity liquid capable of penetrating fabrics and carrying away oils and grime. When depressurized, it reverts to a gas, leaving clothes clean and dry. No wastewater. No dryer.

Beyond its novelty, the idea could clean up a resource-intensive chore. The average family runs roughly 300 loads a year, consuming thousands of gallons of water. And more than 80 percent of U.S. households own a dryer, with one study putting the annual CO2 emissions from machine drying alone at 27 million metric tons.

Long confined to industrial operations, liquid-CO2 cleaning is getting a second look from appliance giants LG and Samsung — this time for the home. Still, shrinking a technology built around bulky, high-pressure machinery to fit both a laundry room and household budget is a tall order. No less challenging is doing so without washing away the environmental gains that make waterless, dryerless laundry so enticing in the first place.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Just getting this far has taken decades. Hughes Aircraft developed the process in 1990 to remove grease and other contaminants from electronic components. Electrolux later pursued it as a safer alternative to solvent-based dry cleaning, though cost, complexity, and bulky equipment kept it from catching on.

In 2009, Colorado-based Tersus Solutions began refining the technology and has since carved out a niche cleaning outdoor apparel and equipment, as well as firefighter gear contaminated with hazardous residues. Its machines offer a glimpse of what CO2 cleaning can do and why squeezing it into a household appliance is no simple feat.

Tersus CEO Peter Whitcomb describes the machines as “futuristic front-loading washers,” though the company’s two models dwarf those found in a typical laundromat. Each occupies a roughly 10-foot cube, with the larger unit handling up to 85 pounds of laundry, or a dozen sleeping bags. Behind a thick, submarine-like hatch, a rotating drum sits inside a pressurized chamber amid a maze of pipes, pumps, and compressors.

Despite the complexity, what happens inside is relatively simple. Carbon dioxide turns from gas to liquid at 900 pounds per square inch of pressure — roughly one third of what’s inside a full scuba tank. As it circulates, filters trap the grime, which accumulates as a thick purplish sludge for disposal. When the 45-minute cycle ends, the pressure drops and liquid returns to gas, instantly drying the load. More than 90 percent of the CO2 is recaptured for the next run; the rest escapes in a smoky wisp.

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The process is particularly effective on firefighter gear, with tests showing an average of more than 95 percent removal of contaminants such as PAHs, potentially harmful compounds found in smoke and soot. Water-soluble stains from sweat and food can be trickier, said Chris Robbins, Tersus’s chief technology officer, occasionally requiring pretreatment — “think Tide pen, but for CO2” — or conventional washing.

For most loads, however, the process eliminates water and additives alike. “We’re not using detergent, we don’t use heat,” Whitcomb said. Tersus estimates its larger machines save roughly 300 gallons of water per load compared with conventional washing. There is another potential upside, as well: By eliminating wastewater and trapping shed fibers for disposal, the process could further reduce microplastic contamination from laundry.

The energy equation, however, is more complicated. A California Energy Commission demonstration with the U.S. Navy found the method used about 15 percent less energy than smaller commercial washers and dryers, yet about as much as larger industrial combinations. Tersus has found comparable performance, said Robbins. While CO2 cleaning avoids thermal drying — typically the most energy-intensive part of conventional laundry — removing impurities from the carbon dioxide for reuse requires significant power. The company is exploring more efficient ways of heating and cooling the gas, Robbins said.

As for the CO2, Tersus gets it from a nearby ethanol plant, where it’s a byproduct of fermentation. That minimizes transportation needs, although purifying and liquefying it require additional energy — further complicating the calculation of the technology’s overall carbon footprint.

Tersus Solutions’ industrial CO₂ washers use high pressure to turn carbon dioxide into a liquid that can clean fabrics without water. The machines’ bulky pressure chambers, pumps, pipes, and compressors illustrate the challenge appliance makers face in trying to shrink the technology for household use. Courtesy Teresus Solutions

Then there’s the question of scale: Could all that machinery — enough to fill a small bedroom — be shrunk into a household appliance?

LG and Samsung are working on that. Recent patents from the companies, both of which declined to comment, tackle distinct challenges: removing stains resistant to CO2 cleaning and reducing the pressure required to make the tech work.

LG’s design uses detergents and other additives to help remove water-soluble stains. Although the patent doesn’t specify a formula, a recent study found that adding isopropyl alcohol and water improved liquid carbon dioxide’s ability to sugars, salts, and other compounds. Samsung, meanwhile, proposes combining CO2 with other solvents to bring operating pressures down to a fraction of those used in industrial machines. That could make home models more compact, though some of the mixtures include PFAS, raising questions about environmental trade-offs.

Smaller, however, doesn’t necessarily mean simpler. Separating and recovering those added solvents could require still more equipment, said Eckhard Groll, head of mechanical engineering at Purdue University and an expert in CO2 refrigeration. “There’s no question” that a home version is technically feasible, he said, “but it may be very costly, the technology.”

Even if the machines become affordable, the environmental benefits may not carry over, said Rainer Stamminger, a household appliance efficiency researcher at the University of Bonn. With households running just a few loads a week, pressurizing and recovering carbon dioxide could be “very inefficient just for one wash” compared to industrial machines that run continuously.

The economics may be especially challenging in the U.S., where electricity is relatively cheap. Groll pointed to heat pump dryers, which use about half the energy of conventional electric models. Popular in Europe, they made up 75 percent of new dryer sales in 2020, helped by higher electricity prices that helped ease the sticker shock; meanwhile, American sales still lag. CO2 washers could as well if their efficiency comes with a hefty upfront premium.

Whitcomb sees greater opportunities in commercial dry cleaning, apartment buildings, and institutions, where higher volumes could justify the equipment costs — and keep the machines running often enough to take advantage of their scale. With a new facility in Calgary expanding its Colorado operations, Tersus now works with more than 40 brands and retailers, offering repairs, restoration, and resale services that “complement the cleaning” to extend garment life and keep products in circulation, Whitcomb said.

Even if engineers can make a home CO2 washer affordable and efficient, they would still have to convince people to buy one. The early market for water-efficient front-load washers offers a precedent: Energy and water savings attracted some consumers, while upfront costs deterred others. Performance and convenience mattered, too, said Gwendolyn Hustvedt, a textiles and consumer sciences professor at Texas State University who studied the trend.

The technology may have one big selling point, however: The clothes come out dry. Beyond saving time and hassle, skipping what Hustvedt called “cooking your clothes in a box” could help garments last longer by reducing shrinkage and wear from heat and tumbling. Whether consumers would pay a premium for those benefits is another question.

Home CO2 washers still have a long way to go before they break up the familiar washer-dryer combo. But if engineers can make the physics work economically — and environmentally — at household scale, the next big thing in laundry might be one less appliance.

The story is focused, detailed, and presents a meaningful environmental breakthrough with broad implications.
articles.personality_title: New laundry machines could clean clothes using carbon dioxide instead of water
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Washing clothes usually needs lots of water and heat to dry, which uses a lot of energy and creates pollution. Scientists and companies have been looking for ways to make laundry easier on the environment.

**What happened** – A special technology that uses liquid carbon dioxide (CO2) to clean clothes without water or heat is being developed for home use. This idea started in the 1990s for cleaning airplane parts and has been used in factories and for cleaning firefighter gear. Now, big companies like LG and Samsung are trying to make smaller machines that people can use at home.

**Impact** – Using CO2 to wash clothes could save thousands of gallons of water each year and reduce the energy used by dryers. It also helps stop tiny plastic fibers from clothes from polluting water. The clothes come out clean and dry without detergent or heat, which could make them last longer.

**What's next step** – The challenge is to shrink the big, heavy machines into smaller, affordable ones for homes. Companies are working on solving problems like removing tough stains and lowering the pressure needed to use CO2 safely. If successful, this could change how people do laundry worldwide.

**One-sentence takeaway** – New washing machines using carbon dioxide instead of water and heat could make laundry cleaner, save water and energy, and help protect the environment.

articles.title: Experts explore returning beavers to River Waveney
articles.summary: A trust says the river-dwelling mammals could improve the health of the waterway.
articles.content:
A river separating two counties could become home to beavers as work begins to explore where a colony could be introduced.

The River Waveney Trust is in conversation with Natural England and other agencies about potentially reintroducing the river-dwelling mammals along the River Waveney.

The 59-mile (95km) waterway rises in Redgrave and Lopham Fen in Suffolk and heads east, creating a border between Norfolk and Suffolk as it flows out into the River Yare at Great Yarmouth.

Ange Lamb, catchment resilience officer, said the upper reaches of the River Waveney and its tributaries could make ideal environments for beavers. If successful, beavers could return by 2029.

Known as river engineers, beavers were native to Britain but they were hunted to extinction by the end of the 16th century.

Conservationists want to reintroduce them to help boost the health of waterways through their ability to create wetland areas.

But there are concerns, particularly around dams being built in inappropriate places and their ability to destroy trees.
articles.reasoning: The article reports on a conservation effort to reintroduce beavers to the River Waveney, which can significantly improve waterway health and ecosystem resilience. This has broad environmental benefits and is a meaningful ecological restoration project with clear substance and potential large-scale impact.
articles.personality_title: Experts consider bringing beavers back to River Waveney
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – The River Waveney, a 59-mile waterway forming a border between Norfolk and Suffolk in England, once had native beavers. These animals disappeared over 400 years ago because they were hunted.

**What happened** – The River Waveney Trust is working with Natural England and other groups to see if beavers can be safely reintroduced to the river. They believe parts of the river and its smaller streams could be good homes for beavers. If all goes well, beavers might return by 2029.

**Impact** – Beavers are known as "river engineers" because they build dams and create wetlands. These changes help clean water, support other wildlife, and improve the river’s health. Returning beavers to the River Waveney could bring these benefits back to the area. However, some people worry about beavers building dams in the wrong places or cutting down too many trees.

**What's next step** – Experts will continue studying where beavers could live without causing problems. They will work with local communities and environmental groups to plan the best way to bring beavers back safely.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Plans are underway to reintroduce beavers to the River Waveney to help restore the river’s natural health and support wildlife by 2029.

articles.title: Who needs sex? Kelp reproduce asexually when no mate is nearby
articles.summary: Nature, Published online: 12 November 2026; doi:10.1038/d41586-026-03665-0Insights into the reproductive modes of brown algae could help in the fight to protect them in warming climate.
articles.content:
Both male and female kelp were shown to be capable of reproduction without fertilization.Credit: Madelein_Wolf/Getty

When potential mates are scarce, some types of seaweed can take reproduction into their own hands, so to speak, according to a study published on 12 November in PLoS Biology1.

“Our findings highlight that kelp are even more flexible in their reproduction than previously appreciated,” says Daniel Liesner, a marine biologist at the GEOMAR Helmholtz Centre for Ocean Research Kiel in Germany.

The brown algae, which provide food and shelter for marine life, “are really weird, they do all kinds of stuff”, says Reina Veenhof, an ecologist at the Scottish Association for Marine Science in Oban, UK. What’s interesting about the study is that it helps to explain how changes in gene activity allow kelp to reproduce in different ways, she says.

Developmental flexibility

Scientists know that kelp can reproduce asexually, with unfertilized eggs developing into offspring. This process was even documented for one male strain2 — the PLoS Biology study shows that this wasn’t a one-off.

The ability of male reproductive cells to develop without fertilization is striking, says Olivier De Clerck, a seaweed biologist at Ghent University in Belgium. This is because, unlike eggs, sperm cells are small and have few resources to support development.

The researchers focused on Laminaria pallida, a species found along the Atlantic coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the wild, 523 individual kelp showed no clear evidence of asexual reproduction.

By contrast, both microscopic male and female L. pallida grown in separate laboratory dishes could produce offspring without fertilization. During asexual reproduction, the gene expression in males changed, making them more similar to females.

However, when they were lab-grown in the presence of a member of the opposite sex, kelp favoured sexual reproduction, suggesting they can detect nearby partners through chemical signals.
articles.reasoning: The article reports a scientific discovery about kelp's flexible reproductive strategies, including asexual reproduction by both male and female kelp. This insight has significant implications for kelp conservation and resilience in warming oceans, benefiting marine ecosystems broadly.
articles.personality_title: Kelp can reproduce alone when no mate is nearby
articles.personality_presentation:
**Context** – Kelp are large brown algae that live in the ocean and provide food and shelter for many sea creatures. Scientists have known that kelp can reproduce in different ways, but they wanted to learn more about how they do this, especially when mates are hard to find.

**What happened** – A new study found that both male and female kelp can reproduce without fertilization, meaning they can create offspring on their own. Researchers studied a kelp species called Laminaria pallida from the coasts of South Africa and Namibia. In the lab, when male and female kelp were grown apart, both could produce new kelp without needing a partner. When grown together, they preferred to reproduce sexually.

**Impact** – This discovery shows kelp are more flexible than we thought. Male kelp, which usually produce tiny sperm cells, can switch their genes to act like females and reproduce alone. This helps kelp survive and keep growing even if there aren’t many mates around. Since kelp forests support many ocean animals, this flexibility could help protect these ecosystems as the climate warms.

**What's next step** – Scientists want to study more kelp species to see if they can also reproduce this way. Understanding how kelp adapt to changing environments can help efforts to protect kelp forests and the animals that depend on them.

**One-sentence takeaway** – Kelp can reproduce without a mate by changing their reproductive cells, helping them survive when partners are scarce.
articles.personality_title_fr: Le varech peut se reproduire seul quand aucun partenaire n’est proche
articles.personality_presentation_fr:
**Contexte** – Le varech est une grande algue brune qui vit dans l’océan et fournit nourriture et abri à de nombreux animaux marins. Les scientifiques savaient que le varech pouvait se reproduire de différentes façons, mais voulaient en savoir plus sur ce mécanisme, surtout quand il y a peu de partenaires.

**Ce qui s’est passé** – Une nouvelle étude a montré que les varechs mâles et femelles peuvent se reproduire sans fécondation, c’est-à-dire qu’ils peuvent avoir une descendance seuls. Les chercheurs ont étudié une espèce appelée Laminaria pallida, originaire des côtes d’Afrique du Sud et de Namibie. En laboratoire, quand les varechs mâles et femelles étaient séparés, ils pouvaient produire de nouveaux varechs sans partenaire. Quand ils étaient ensemble, ils préféraient la reproduction sexuelle.

**Impact** – Cette découverte montre que le varech est plus flexible qu’on ne le pensait. Les varechs mâles, qui produisent normalement de petites cellules reproductrices, peuvent changer l’expression de leurs gènes pour agir comme des femelles et se reproduire seuls. Cela aide le varech à survivre et à se développer même quand il y a peu de partenaires. Comme les forêts de varech soutiennent beaucoup d’animaux marins, cette flexibilité pourrait aider à protéger ces écosystèmes face au réchauffement climatique.

**Prochaine étape** – Les scientifiques veulent étudier d’autres espèces de varech pour voir si elles peuvent aussi se reproduire ainsi. Comprendre comment le varech s’adapte aux changements peut aider à mieux protéger ces forêts et les animaux qui en dépendent.

**Résumé en une phrase** – Le varech peut se reproduire sans partenaire en modifiant ses cellules reproductrices, ce qui lui permet de survivre quand les partenaires manquent.
articles.personality_title_es: El alga marina puede reproducirse sola cuando no hay pareja cerca
articles.personality_presentation_es:
**Contexto** – El alga marina, o kelp, es un tipo de alga marrón grande que vive en el océano y ofrece alimento y refugio a muchos animales marinos. Los científicos sabían que el kelp puede reproducirse de varias formas, pero querían entender mejor cómo lo hace cuando no hay parejas cercanas.

**Qué pasó** – Un nuevo estudio descubrió que tanto el kelp macho como el hembra pueden reproducirse sin fertilización, es decir, pueden crear descendencia por sí solos. Los investigadores estudiaron una especie llamada Laminaria pallida, que vive en las costas de Sudáfrica y Namibia. En el laboratorio, cuando los kelp macho y hembra se cultivaron separados, ambos pudieron producir nuevos kelp sin necesidad de pareja. Cuando se cultivaron juntos, prefirieron reproducirse sexualmente.

**Impacto** – Este hallazgo muestra que el kelp es más flexible de lo que se pensaba. El kelp macho, que normalmente produce células reproductivas pequeñas llamadas espermatozoides, puede cambiar la actividad de sus genes para actuar como hembra y reproducirse solo. Esto ayuda al kelp a sobrevivir y crecer aun cuando faltan parejas. Como los bosques de kelp sostienen a muchos animales marinos, esta flexibilidad podría ayudar a proteger estos ecosistemas a medida que el clima cambia.

**Próximo paso** – Los científicos quieren estudiar más especies de kelp para ver si también pueden reproducirse de esta manera. Entender cómo se adaptan puede ayudar a proteger mejor los bosques de kelp y a los animales que dependen de ellos.

**Resumen en una frase** – El kelp puede reproducirse sin pareja al cambiar sus células reproductivas, lo que le permite sobrevivir cuando faltan compañeros.
